usage: Use 잔 for cups/glasses of any drink: coffee, water, beer, soju.
Native-Korean numbers (한, 두, 세...) go in front of 잔.
Super common when ordering another round of drinks at a bar.
Spacing: number + space + 잔. Don't write 세잔.
examples: 저는 하루에 커피를 세 잔 마셔요.
I drink three cups of coffee a day.
Number + 잔 acts as the object's amount; the verb stays at the end.
딱 한 잔만 더 할까요?
Shall we have just one more drink?
딱 ... 만 = 'just exactly one'; classic line for one more round.
물 한 잔만 주시겠어요?
Could you give me a glass of water?
Polite request in a cafe or restaurant; 만 softens it to 'just one'.
nuance: 잔 counts servings of liquid in a cup or glass, so it pairs with both hot and cold drinks. With alcohol, '한 잔 더' is shorthand for another round and '한잔하다' (written together as a verb) means 'to grab a drink'. Always use native-Korean numbers (한, 두, 세) directly before 잔.
mistakes: Using Sino-Korean numbers like 일 잔, 이 잔 instead of native 한 잔, 두 잔.
Counting bottles with 잔 — a bottle is 병, while 잔 is only the poured glass/cup.

usage: 켤레 counts things worn in twos: shoes, socks, gloves.
Use native numbers; 한, 두, 세 켤레.
Ask quantity of footwear/socks with 몇 켤레.
Gloves come as a pair, so 켤레 not 개.
examples: 운동화 한 켤레 사고 싶어요.
I want to buy a pair of sneakers.
한 켤레 sits right before the verb as the amount bought.
양말 세 켤레에 오천 원이에요.
Three pairs of socks are 5,000 won.
Common price tag wording at a market or sock shop.
겨울이라 따뜻한 장갑 한 켤레가 필요해요.
Since it's winter, I need a warm pair of gloves.
-이라 gives the reason; 한 켤레가 marks the needed item.
nuance: 켤레 is the standard counter for items naturally worn as a matching pair — shoes, sneakers, socks, and gloves. Use a single 켤레 for the whole pair, never count the left and right separately. Pair it with native-Korean numbers.
mistakes: Counting shoes with 개 (개 is for generic objects); footwear pairs take 켤레.
Saying 두 켤레 for one pair of shoes — one pair is 한 켤레, both shoes together.

usage: 벌 counts full garments or matching sets: a suit, a dress, pajamas.
A suit (jacket + pants) counts as 한 벌.
Ask how many garments with 몇 벌.
examples: 출근용 정장 한 벌을 새로 샀어요.
I bought a new suit for work.
한 벌을 marks the suit as the object; 출근용 = 'for commuting/work'.
이번 여행에 옷 세 벌만 챙겼어요.
I only packed three outfits for this trip.
세 벌만 = 'just three sets'; 챙기다 = to pack/gather.
잠옷 한 벌이 더 있으면 좋겠어요.
I wish I had one more set of pajamas.
한 벌이 더 = 'one more set'; -면 좋겠어요 expresses a wish.
nuance: 벌 counts clothing as a complete garment or coordinated set, so a suit, dress, hanbok, or pajama set is all 한 벌 even when it has multiple pieces. For single small items like a T-shirt you can also use 벌, but 개 or 장 may sound more casual. Use native-Korean numbers with 벌.
mistakes: Counting a two-piece suit as 두 벌 — the matching set is 한 벌.
Using 벌 for shoes; shoes are 켤레, clothing is 벌.

usage: 권 counts books, notebooks, magazines, and bound volumes.
Native numbers go before 권: 한, 두, 세 권.
Ask book quantity with 몇 권.
Each volume of a series is counted separately.
examples: 한 달에 책을 두 권 정도 읽어요.
I read about two books a month.
두 권 정도 = 'about two'; 정도 softens the number to an estimate.
이 소설은 전부 다섯 권이에요.
This novel has five volumes in total.
전부 = 'in total'; series volumes each count as 권.
도서관에서 책 세 권을 빌렸어요.
I borrowed three books from the library.
세 권을 marks the books as the object of 빌리다.
nuance: 권 is the counter for anything bound like a book — novels, textbooks, notebooks, magazines, and each volume of a multi-volume series. It pairs with native-Korean numbers and is one of the most common counters you'll use when talking about reading or studying. Don't confuse it with 장, which counts loose sheets of paper.
mistakes: Using 개 for books instead of 권.
Counting loose pages with 권 — a single sheet is 장, a whole book is 권.

usage: 장 counts flat thin things: paper, tickets, photos, cards.
Movie/transport tickets are counted with 장.
Ask quantity of sheets/tickets with 몇 장.
Thin flat food like 김 also uses 장.
examples: 영화표 두 장 주세요.
Two movie tickets, please.
두 장 sits before 주세요; standard line at a ticket counter.
복사 용지 열 장만 주시겠어요?
Could you give me just ten sheets of copy paper?
열 장만 = 'just ten sheets'; 만 limits the amount.
사진을 한 장 찍어 주시겠어요?
Could you take one photo (for me)?
한 장 counts the photo; common polite request to a passerby.
nuance: 장 counts flat, thin items — sheets of paper, tickets, photos, banknotes, stickers, and even thin foods like dried seaweed or a slice of cheese. It is one of the most frequent counters in daily errands, especially at ticket windows and copy machines. Use native-Korean numbers with it.
mistakes: Counting books with 장 — a bound book is 권; 장 is a single sheet.
Using 개 for tickets instead of the natural 장.

usage: 대 counts vehicles and machines: cars, bikes, phones, computers, ACs.
Native numbers before 대: 한, 두, 세 대.
Ask quantity of machines/vehicles with 몇 대.
Home appliances are counted with 대.
examples: 우리 집에는 차가 한 대 있어요.
There's one car in our household.
차가 한 대 있어요 = 'have one car'; 대 counts the vehicle.
사무실에 컴퓨터가 다섯 대 있어요.
There are five computers in the office.
다섯 대 counts the machines as a quantity.
에어컨 한 대를 더 설치하고 싶어요.
I want to install one more air conditioner.
한 대를 더 = 'one more unit'; 대 fits appliances.
nuance: 대 is the go-to counter for machines and vehicles — cars, motorcycles, bicycles, computers, phones, cameras, TVs, and air conditioners. It covers almost anything mechanical or electronic in the home or office, so a resident uses it constantly when talking about appliances. Pair it with native-Korean numbers.
mistakes: Using 개 for cars or appliances instead of 대.
Counting people who ride in a car with 대 — people are 명, the vehicle is 대.

usage: 채 counts whole houses and buildings.
Native numbers before 채: 한, 두, 세 채.
Ask quantity of houses/buildings with 몇 채.
채 is used when counting an apartment as a whole property.
examples: 이 동네에 새 아파트가 두 채 생겼어요.
Two new apartment buildings went up in this neighborhood.
두 채 counts the buildings; 생기다 = to come into being.
할머니는 시골에 집을 한 채 가지고 계세요.
My grandmother owns a house in the countryside.
한 채 counts the house; 계세요 is honorific 'has/owns'.
저 큰 건물 한 채가 전부 회사예요.
That entire big building is all company offices.
한 채가 전부 = 'one whole building, all of it'; 전부 emphasizes scale.
nuance: 채 counts entire dwellings and sizeable buildings — houses, traditional homes, and apartment buildings or units treated as whole properties. You'll meet it most in real-estate talk and descriptions of neighborhoods. It uses native-Korean numbers and refers to the structure as a whole, not the rooms inside.
mistakes: Counting rooms inside a home with 채 — rooms are 개 (방 한 개); the whole house is 채.
Using 대 (for machines) when you mean a building, which is 채.

english: counter for flowers and clustered fruit
usage: 송이 counts individual blossoms and clusters.
Native numbers before 송이: 한, 두, 세 송이.
Fruit growing in a cluster (grapes, bananas) uses 송이.
Ask quantity of flowers with 몇 송이.
examples: 장미 한 송이만 주세요.
Just one rose, please.
한 송이만 = 'just one bloom'; common at a flower shop.
포도 한 송이에 만 원이에요.
One bunch of grapes is 10,000 won.
송이 counts the grape cluster; typical fruit-stand pricing.
여자친구한테 꽃 열 송이를 선물했어요.
I gave my girlfriend ten flowers as a gift.
열 송이를 marks the flowers; -한테 = 'to (a person)'.
nuance: 송이 counts single blossoms and naturally clustered produce — a rose, a tulip, a bunch of grapes or bananas. For a wrapped bouquet you'd switch to 다발, but each separate stem or cluster is 송이. It takes native-Korean numbers and shows up whenever you buy flowers or fruit.
mistakes: Using 개 for a single flower instead of the natural 송이.
Confusing 송이 (a single bloom/cluster) with 다발 (a bound bouquet).

english: counter for rows, lines, and strips (e.g. gimbap)
usage: 줄 counts long things in a line: a gimbap roll, a row, a line of text.
Native numbers before 줄: 한, 두, 세 줄.
한 줄로 서다 = 'line up in one row'.
Ask quantity of lines with 몇 줄.
examples: 김밥 두 줄 포장해 주세요.
Please pack two rolls of gimbap to go.
두 줄 counts the gimbap rolls; 포장 = takeout packing.
여기 한 줄로 서 주세요.
Please line up in a single line here.
한 줄로 = 'in one line'; common queue instruction.
이 글을 두 줄로 요약해 봤어요.
I summarized this text in two lines.
두 줄로 = 'in two lines'; 줄 counts lines of writing.
nuance: 줄 counts things arranged in a long line — a roll of gimbap, a row of seats, a queue of people, or lines of text. It is the everyday counter for ordering gimbap and for telling people how to line up. Use native-Korean numbers, and note 한 줄로 서다 ('stand in one line') is a set phrase you'll hear often.
mistakes: Counting gimbap pieces (slices) with 줄 — the whole uncut roll is 한 줄, slices are 개.
Using 개 for a queue or row when 줄 is the natural counter.

usage: 마리 counts all animals: pets, fish, birds, insects.
Native numbers before 마리: 한, 두, 세 마리.
Ask animal quantity with 몇 마리.
A whole (cooked) chicken is also counted with 마리.
examples: 저는 고양이를 두 마리 키워요.
I have two cats.
두 마리 counts the cats; 키우다 = to raise/keep a pet.
치킨 한 마리 시킬까요?
Shall we order one whole chicken?
한 마리 counts the chicken; classic fried-chicken order.
공원에서 새 세 마리를 봤어요.
I saw three birds in the park.
세 마리를 marks the birds as what was seen.
nuance: 마리 is the universal counter for animals — dogs, cats, fish, birds, insects, and even a whole cooked chicken at a fried-chicken place. It applies to creatures regardless of size, so the same word counts an ant and an elephant. Use native-Korean numbers, and remember people are counted with 명, not 마리.
mistakes: Counting people with 마리 — people take 명 (마리 for a person is rude/joking).
Using 개 for animals instead of 마리.

usage: 끼 counts meal occasions: breakfast, lunch, dinner.
Native numbers before 끼: 한, 두, 세 끼.
Ask meal count with 몇 끼.
to make do with one meal
한 끼 + 때우다 = grab a quick meal.
examples: 보통 하루에 세 끼를 먹어요.
I usually eat three meals a day.
세 끼를 counts the meals as the object of 먹다.
바빠서 오늘 한 끼밖에 못 먹었어요.
I was so busy I only ate one meal today.
한 끼밖에 + 못 = 'only one meal'; 밖에 needs a negative verb.
저녁 한 끼는 가볍게 먹으려고 해요.
I'm trying to eat one light meal for dinner.
한 끼는 marks the meal; -려고 해요 = 'plan/try to'.
nuance: 끼 counts meal occasions rather than dishes — one sitting of breakfast, lunch, or dinner is 한 끼. It's the natural way to talk about eating habits, skipping meals, or meal plans. Use native-Korean numbers, and note the set phrase 한 끼 때우다 ('grab a quick bite to get by').
mistakes: Counting individual dishes with 끼 — a dish/plate is 개 or 그릇; 끼 is a whole meal sitting.
Using Sino-Korean numbers (일 끼) instead of native 한 끼, 두 끼.

usage: 군데 counts locations or spots: shops, sites, sore spots.
Native numbers before 군데: 한, 두, 세 군데.
Very common: 몇 군데 = 'how many spots'.
examples: 병원을 세 군데나 가 봤어요.
I even went to three different hospitals.
세 군데나 = 'as many as three places'; 나 stresses the number.
집을 두 군데 보고 결정할게요.
I'll look at two places and then decide.
두 군데 counts the homes/locations to view.
몸이 여러 군데 아파요.
I ache in several spots on my body.
여러 군데 = 'in several places'; 군데 counts sore spots too.
nuance: 군데 counts locations or spots — shops you visited, apartments you toured, or places on the body that hurt. It's especially handy with 몇 군데 ('how many places') and 여러 군데 ('several places') when comparing options or describing scattered pain. Use native-Korean numbers, and note 곳 is a close synonym that's slightly more formal.
mistakes: Using 개 for places instead of the natural 군데 (or 곳).
Mixing up 군데 with 군대 (military/army) — different word entirely.
